title: Medical Abbreviations and Unsafe-Abbreviation Awareness

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify common approved medical abbreviations and their meanings used in clinical documentation.
- Recognize error-prone and 'do not use' abbreviations that increase the risk of medication and documentation errors.
- Explain how ambiguous abbreviations lead to miscommunication and why clarifying them protects patient safety.
- Apply correct safe-writing practices, including leading zeros, written-out units, and approved alternatives, in office documentation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

BP is short for blood pressure — how hard your blood pushes against your blood vessel walls, like the water pressure in a garden hose.

### Question 2

HR stands for heart rate — how many times your heart beats in one minute, like counting how many times a drum is hit in 60 seconds.

### Question 3

RR is respiratory rate — how many breaths you take in a minute, like counting how many times a balloon fills and empties.

### Question 4

Hx is a shortcut for "history" — the story of a person's health so far, like a timeline of everything important that happened before today.

### Question 5

Dx means diagnosis — the doctor's name for what is making a person sick, like labeling a mystery to explain the clues.

### Question 6

Rx is a very old shortcut for "prescription" — it is the sign you see on a pharmacy sign, meaning medicine a doctor has ordered.

### Question 7

CC is the main reason a person came to the doctor — like the headline of a news story, telling everyone the most important point right away.

### Question 8

NKA means the patient says they are not allergic to any medicines or things we know about — like a blank "no allergies" box on a form.

### Question 9

PMH is like a person's health scrapbook of everything that has happened to them medically before this visit.

### Question 10

FH is the health story of a person's relatives — like looking at what runs in a family tree, such as heart problems or diabetes.

### Question 11

ROS is like going through a checklist of every part of the body — eyes, ears, heart, stomach — to see if anything feels off.

### Question 12

SOAP is a recipe for writing a good doctor's note: what the patient says, what we measure, what we think is wrong, and what we will do next.

### Question 13

VS means vital signs — the important numbers like temperature, pulse, breathing, and blood pressure that tell us how a body is working.

### Question 14

PRN means "take it only when you need it," like taking pain medicine only when something actually hurts, not on a fixed clock.

### Question 15

PO means the medicine goes in the mouth, like swallowing a pill or drinking a liquid.

### Question 16

NPO means the patient should not eat or drink anything, like a sign on a snack cabinet that says "no snacking before this test."

### Question 17

STAT means "right now, no waiting" — like a fire alarm that tells everyone to act at once.

### Question 18

BID means twice a day, like brushing your teeth in the morning and again at night.

### Question 19

TID means three times a day, like eating breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

### Question 20

QID means four times a day, like taking medicine with breakfast, lunch, dinner, and at bedtime.

### Question 21

AC means before meals — like taking a medicine on an empty stomach before you eat breakfast.

### Question 22

PC means after meals, like taking a medicine right after you finish eating.

### Question 23

mg means milligram — a tiny unit for weighing medicine, like a very small pinch of salt on a scale.

### Question 24

mL means milliliter — a small amount of liquid, like the amount in a medicine cup or a teaspoon.

### Question 25

mcg means microgram — an even tinier amount than a milligram, like comparing a single grain of sugar to a whole spoonful.

### Question 26

q2h means "every two hours," like checking the clock every two hours to take your medicine.

### Question 27

OTC means "over the counter" — medicine you can buy off the shelf at the store without a doctor's note.

### Question 28

c/o means "complains of" — it is shorthand for what the patient says is bothering them.

### Question 29

N/V means nausea and vomiting — feeling sick to your stomach and throwing up.

### Question 30

SOB means shortness of breath — feeling like you cannot get enough air.

### Question 31

Abd is short for abdomen — the belly area, where your stomach and other organs live.

### Question 32

w/o means "without" — it is shorthand for something being absent, like "pain w/o fever."

### Question 33

F/U means "follow-up" — coming back to the doctor later to check on how things are going.

### Question 34

CBC is a "complete blood count" — a test that counts the different kinds of cells in your blood.

### Question 35

UA means urinalysis — testing a sample of pee to look for signs of infection or other problems.

### Question 36

EKG and ECG are two names for the same test that draws a picture of the heart's electricity, like a heartbeat scribble on paper.

### Question 37

Hct (hematocrit) tells how much of your blood is made of red blood cells, like measuring how much fruit is in a smoothie.

### Question 38

Reading this note is like decoding a short secret message: "headache for 2 days, sick stomach, no fever, and their important numbers look fine."

### Question 39

The letter "U" can look like a zero, so we write the whole word "unit" instead — like printing your name clearly so no one misreads it.

### Question 40

IU looks like the letters IV, so a nurse might think the medicine should go into a vein instead of being measured in units — we write the full words to stay safe.

### Question 41

QD means once a day, but if the little "I" is missing or added, it can turn into QID — four times a day. That is why we write "daily" instead.

### Question 42

QOD is supposed to mean "every other day," but it is so easy to misread as "every day" or "four times a day" that we just write the words out.

### Question 43

Writing "1.0" is risky because the little dot can be missed and "1.0" becomes "10." We write just "1" to be safe.

### Question 44

Putting a zero before the dot (0.5) is like putting a bright flag in front of the dot so no one misses it and reads "5" by mistake.

### Question 45

The symbol for microgram looks like it could be an "m" for milligram, and those are 1,000 times different — so we write "mcg" to be clear.

### Question 46

cc was an old word for a small amount of liquid, but it can be misread, so we say "mL" instead — same idea, safer letters.

### Question 47

MS could mean two very different medicines, like two kids with the same nickname — so we write out the full name to know which one we mean.

### Question 48

MSO4 and MgSO4 look like twins with one letter different, but one is a strong pain medicine and the other is a mineral medicine — writing full names keeps them apart.

### Question 49

AS and OS look almost the same, but one means "ear" and the other means "eye." Writing "left ear" or "left eye" avoids mixing them up.

### Question 50

OD can mean "right eye" or "once a day," which are very different things — writing the words out makes the meaning obvious.

### Question 51

SC and SQ look like they could mean "under the tongue" (SL) instead of "under the skin," so we write "subcut" to be clear.

### Question 52

D/C is like one key that opens two different doors — "go home" or "stop this medicine" — so we write the whole word to pick the right door.

### Question 53

HS might mean "half as strong" or "at bedtime," which are totally different — writing the words out tells everyone which one you mean.

### Question 54

TIW is meant to be "three times a week," but it is easy to read wrong, so we write the words to be sure.

### Question 55

OJ (orange juice) looks like the letters for "right eye" or "left eye," so we write "orange juice" to avoid mix-ups.

### Question 56

BT (bedtime) and BID (twice a day) look a lot alike, so we write "bedtime" to keep them apart.

### Question 57

The "@" sign can look like the number 2, so we write the little word "at" instead.

### Question 58

The pointy signs > and < can look like a 7 or an L, so we write "greater than" or "less than" in words.

### Question 59

The squiggly "&" sign just means "and," so we write the simple word "and" instead.

### Question 60

ss (short for sliding scale insulin) can look like the number 55, so we write "sliding scale" to be safe.

### Question 61

IJ (injection) looks like IV (into a vein), so we write the full word to avoid giving a medicine the wrong way.

### Question 62

If a note has risky shortcuts, the safe move is to ask the person who wrote it to say it clearly — never to guess.

### Question 63

q1d is a cramped way to say "once a day," and the number can be misread — so we just write "daily."

### Question 64

Old-fashioned symbols like "dram" and "minim" are like using a secret code few people know — we use clear metric units like mL instead.

### Question 65

x3d is supposed to mean "for 3 days," but someone might read it as "take 3 doses," so we write the words out.

### Question 66

When you copy "2.5," if the little dot gets lost, it becomes "25" — ten times bigger. That is why we copy slowly and double-check.

### Question 67

Writing "0.5" with the zero in front is like putting a guard in front of the dot so it cannot be missed.

### Question 68

If the letter U looks like a zero, "10 U" can become "100" — ten times too much medicine. That is why we write "units."

### Question 69

MSO4 and MgSO4 are like two nearly identical passwords — one wrong letter opens the wrong door, so we spell out the full drug name.

### Question 70

Once a day (QD) accidentally becoming four times a day (QID) is like pouring four cups instead of one — way too much medicine.

### Question 71

The extra zero after the dot (1.0) is like leaving a trap — if the dot is missed, 1 becomes 10. We leave the zero off.

### Question 72

Writing ".5" is like hiding the decimal point; add the zero in front (0.5) so the dot cannot be missed.

### Question 73

If you cannot tell what a note means, the safe rule is to ask the person who wrote it — never to guess, even with a friend's help.

### Question 74

For orders given out loud, repeat them back and ask for any confusing shortcuts to be spelled out — like repeating a phone number to be sure.

### Question 75

Having one agreed-upon list of safe shortcuts is like one shared dictionary — everyone reads words the same way.

### Question 76

NPO is doctor shorthand for "nothing to eat or drink." The assistant explains it in everyday words so the patient understands.

### Question 77

Using full, clear words is like everyone speaking the same language — fewer chances for someone to misunderstand.

### Question 78

D/C is one abbreviation with two very different meanings — like "stop" or "go home." When it is unclear, ask before doing anything.

### Question 79

The best protection is simple: write neatly, use only the approved shortcuts, and ask when something is not clear.

### Question 80

Writing "0.125" keeps the zero in front and leaves off extra zeros at the end — the safest way to write a small dose.

### Question 81

QD and QID are like "cat" and "cats" — one tiny letter changes everything, so we avoid both and write "daily" or "four times a day."

### Question 82

If a teammate keeps using an old, risky shortcut, the right move is to use the safe word yourself and kindly encourage them to do the same.

### Question 83

The ISMP list is like a "watch out" list of tricky shortcuts and the safe words to use instead.

### Question 84

Ear and eye shortcuts look like twins, so a drop meant for an ear could go into an eye — writing "left ear" or "right eye" stops the mix-up.

### Question 85

The golden rule is simple: use the shortcuts everyone agrees on, and spell out or ask about anything that could be misunderstood.
